result.question:
One of the recent oil samples from Transformer 1 at site MAIN shows a jump in hydrogen. Before anyone acts on it, I want to rule out a bad sample. A sample that picked up air during handling usually shows oxygen and nitrogen jumping at the same time.

Between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, screen hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen for anomalous samples with a proper anomaly detection model, not a fixed threshold. For each gas, list the flagged timestamps and their values. Mark a flagged hydrogen sample as 'suspect' if oxygen or nitrogen is also flagged at the same timestamp. Otherwise mark it as 'genuine'.

Then build a second finding from the latest complete sample that isn't suspect. A complete sample has all of the following present:
- hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene
- co, co2, oxygen and nitrogen
- dbds, interfacial_v and dielectric_rigidity

From that sample, give me:
- a dissolved gas fault classification from the five fault gases
- a health index and condition category from all twelve inputs

If the newest sample is itself suspect, say so, use the previous complete sample, and give me its timestamp.

Decide as follows:
- **Sampling artefact.** Every hydrogen flag is suspect, the class is not D1, D2 or T3, and the health index is fair or better. First check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing oil sampling job. If one exists, give me its number and don't duplicate it. Otherwise, create a priority 3 resample work order. In its notes, list the suspect timestamps and ask for a gas-tight syringe.
- **Real fault.** At least one hydrogen flag is genuine and the class is PD, D1 or D2. Check open work orders the same way. If there's no match, create a priority 2 work order covering a confirmatory oil sample and a partial discharge investigation. Code it with the closest discharge failure code from our catalog.
- **Disagreement.** The two findings disagree, for example a genuine hydrogen flag with a mild class, or only suspect flags with a D1, D2 or T3 class or a poor health index. Don't create a corrective job. Recommend a confirmatory resample within 7 days and tell me which finding disagreed.
- **Nothing flagged.** If hydrogen isn't flagged at all, say the window looks stable and create nothing.

If any of hydrogen, oxygen or nitrogen has fewer than 4 non-null samples, skip the model for that gas. Instead, flag any sample more than 50% above that gas's window mean as a manual outlier, and say so. If an input for the health index is missing in every candidate sample, don't estimate it. Name the missing input and base the decision on the gas classification alone.
result.answer:
I couldn't finish this as specified. The anomaly model never ran, and the fault-classification tool failed twice. I created no work order, because none of your four outcomes can be picked without those results.

**1. Anomaly screen (not run)**
- There are 4 samples in the window, one a day from 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-18. Each gas has 4 non-null values, so the 50%-above-mean fallback doesn't apply and a model was required.
- The anomaly tools only read data from a file. Direct IoT links and inline data were both rejected, and none of my tools can write a file. The catalog also has no anomaly detection models registered.

So I have no flagged timestamps and no suspect or genuine labels. For reference only, not as a substitute for the model, here are the raw values:

| Timestamp | H₂ | O₂ | N₂ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-15 | 2845 | 5860 | 27842 |
| 2024-01-16 | 2950 | 5700 | 28000 |
| 2024-01-17 | 2800 | 5900 | 27700 |
| 2024-01-18 | 2900 | 5800 | 27950 |

Hydrogen stays within about ±3% of its window mean (2874). Its highest point, 2950 on 01-16, came with the lowest oxygen reading, not an oxygen jump, so this doesn't look like a sample that picked up air. The run log shows earlier anomaly runs on Transformer 1 today: most flagged nothing, and one flagged position 1 of 4. I can't confirm which gas or window those runs used, so I haven't relied on them.

**2. Latest complete sample: 2024-01-18T00:00:00**
All twelve inputs are present. No sample was marked suspect, because the screen didn't run.
- **Health index:** 71.9, condition **Good**.
- **Fault classification:** the tool returned "LLM unavailable" twice, so there is none. My own hand calculation of the Rogers ratios gives code 0-2-2, a high-temperature thermal fault (T2 or T3; at a ratio of 3.05 it sits on the border). That is my estimate, not a tool result.

**Decision:** If a working screen confirms no hydrogen flags, this becomes "Nothing flagged": the window is stable and nothing gets created. But if the fault classification comes back as T3, it points to a thermal fault that deserves attention whatever the sampling result.

To finish, I need the gas data saved as a file the anomaly tools can read, and the fault-classification tool back online. I can then run the screen and apply your rules.

It did not run tsfm.data_quality, did not execute tsfm.run_recipe with task 'tsfm_anomaly_detection' (an inline sktime detector such as SubLOF was available per recipe_template even though find_models returned no catalog models), and so produced no flagged timestamps or suspect/genuine labels. fmsr.interpret_dga was reported as failing twice and the agent substituted a hand-calculated Rogers ratio, which it did clearly label as its own estimate rather than a tool result; the health index (71.9, Good) is reported but the call is not visible in the truncated log. No work-order check (wo.list_workorders) or decision branch was applied. The agent should have retried the anomaly recipe with a dataset_path approach (e.g., using any available save/materialize mechanism or the IoT-to-TSFM handoff), tried the DGA tool again or reported the exact error, checked open work orders regardless, and then applied the decision logic. Credit is given for transparently admitting failure rather than fabricating results.
